text: An alien language uses the same twenty-six lowercase letters, but in a different order, given by a string called order. Given a list of words, return whether they are sorted by this alien order.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — the alien order is given, so I'm not deriving it. I just have to check the words are in non-decreasing order under it. Is that right?

Good, that's the key point. Since the order is given, I can turn it into a rank array — rank of a letter is its position in order. Then comparing two letters is just comparing their ranks. And to check the whole list is sorted, I only need to check each adjacent pair is in order. Are there any constraints on the input size?
Up to a hundred words, each up to twenty characters.

Let me run through the example. Words: word, then world, with order starting w, o, r, l, d. Here l has rank three and d has rank four. The first three letters match, then d versus l: since four is bigger than three, d is bigger, so word should come after world. They're out of order — answer false. Note the alien order flips the normal one, where d comes before l.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to sort a copy of the words with a custom comparator and check it equals the original. That works, but it's n log n times the word length, and it's more than I need — checking is it already sorted is a single linear pass. This problem reminds me of plain dictionary-order comparison, just with letters remapped by rank. One thing I want to flag early: this is not the same as building an unknown order with a topological sort over a letter graph. Here the order is given, so no graph at all.

Here's the plan. One: build rank, each letter's place in the alien order, so a letter comparison is one array lookup. Two: for each adjacent pair, compare column by column; the first different letter decides — bigger rank first means false. Three: if all shared letters match and the first word is longer, return false. One thing worth flagging — why checking adjacent pairs is enough. Sorted-ness is transitive: if word zero is at most word one, and word one is at most word two, then word zero is at most word two for free. So I don't need all n squared pairs. There's a trade-off here. The prefix case is easy to miss: apple before app must be false, because the shorter word should come first. I handle it after the inner loop. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. First I fill rank from order. Then for each adjacent pair I walk up to the shorter length: same letter, keep going; a bigger rank in the first word, return false. After the loop, if j reached the shorter length and the first word is longer, that's the prefix rule — return false. One thing worth flagging — the break is doing real work. Once the first differing letter settles the pair, I must stop. If I kept comparing later columns, a reversed letter further down could wrongly fail a pair that's already in order — like a y then b x, where a ranks before b but y ranks after x.

Let's dry-run the code with an example. The pair word and world, with rank w zero, o one, r two, l three, d four. Expected output is false. The first three columns are equal. At column three, d and l differ. In the alien order d outranks l, four versus three, so word is bigger than world but comes first — out of order, return false. Let's also test with corner cases. App then apple is true — all shared letters match and the shorter word is first. Flip it to apple then app and the prefix check fires: j reaches the shorter length with everything equal, but the first word is longer, so false. A single word is trivially true.

The time complexity is linear in the total length of all words — building rank is twenty-six steps, and every letter I compare is charged once against the total input length. The space complexity is constant — just the fixed twenty-six-slot rank array. In the worst-case scenario, all words nearly equal, I scan every character once. Oh, one more thing — if the alphabet weren't fixed twenty-six lowercase letters, say Unicode, I'd swap the rank array for a hash map. The comparison logic is identical; only the lookup changes.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You separated this cleanly from the unknown-order version up front — the order is given, so no topological sort. You justified checking only adjacent pairs with transitivity, instead of all pairs. And you flagged both easy-to-miss cases: the prefix rule, and why the break is needed so a later column can't wrongly fail a settled pair. Good work.
